newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey not benefiting from customs union - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Turkey not benefiting from customs union - analysts.

text.p: The European Union (EU) rather than Turkey is benefiting from a customs union pact in palce since the start of the year because Ankara lacks political will to bring its laws in line with the EU, Turkish analysts said.

"It is all because of Turkey's approach to the deal. Customs union means inviting the liberal law system, not liberalising the economy," Can Baydarol, associate proffesor in the European Community desk of the Marmara University, told Reuters.
"If Turkey does not take necessary measures to apply the same liberal law system within its borders, this trade gap will remain at its current high level," he added.

Turkey's trade gap with the EU surged 273.7 percent to $2.137 billion in the first quarter of 1996 when compared to the same 1995 period, according to official data which has been delayed by technical difficulties caused by the pact.

On the first anniversary of the European Parliament's approval of the deal, analysts said the customs union should have been a big step towards full membership in the EU and attract foreign investors.

A 35.2 percent drop in foreign investment inflow to Turkey in the first 11 months of 1996 compared to a year ago was another major disappointment after earlier propaganda that the customs union would boost foreign investment.

"(Then prime minister) Tansu Ciller used the customs union idea for her own domestic propaganda before the (December 24) general elections last year," said professor Esfender Korkmaz, dean of economics at Istanbul University.
"And now her party is paying its debts to its coalition partner (Islamist Welfare Party) which is definitely against the EU and the customs union."
Atilla Karaosmanoglu, former vice-president of the World Bank, blamed politicians and bureaucrats "who slackened" after the deal was approved.

Professor Izzettin Onder from Istanbul University's economics faculty said "structural problems of the Turkish economy", such as huge budget and current account deficits and high inflation of around 80 percent were to blame.
"The politicians were protracted by the economy which was not and still is not ready to compete with the European rivals within the customs union deal," he told Reuters.
EU representative Michael Lake was quoted as saying by the Anatolian agency on Wednesday that the results of the pact were "satisfactory".
He said Turkey's food, automotive parts, glass-glassware and electronics industries were positively affected and no major bankruptcies occurred in 1996.
The agency also quoted Reyhan Atmaca, director of EU relations in the Foreign Trade Undersecretariat as saying: "The customs union was a milestone and there is no turning back."
"But the slowdown in Turkey's progress in developing EU relations is undermining the customs union...It must be shown that political will on the customs union still exists," she added.
Turkey has not passed a law to bring its tax system in line with the EU and has not yet formed an anti-monopoly board required as part of the customs union.
On the other hand, European Parliament has frozen financial aid to Turkey, including MEDA funds, citing lack of improvement in its human rights record.
Officials have also said recession in Germany and other major European markets was the main reason behind a drop in Turkey's leading export item readywear this year.
